name: Three-quarter view
blurb: Turned about 45 degrees: the most popular angle for faces, portraits and character art
title: Three-Quarter View (3/4 View): Face & Body Drawing Reference
description: Three-quarter view (3/4 view) reference: how to draw a face turned about 45 degrees, where the far eye and cheek go, and why photographers love this angle.
answer: A three-quarter view, or 3/4 view, shows a face or body turned roughly 45 degrees from the viewer, halfway between front view and side profile. You see the full near side of the face and part of the far side, which gives a strong sense of depth while keeping both eyes visible.

sections.h: Why the 3/4 view is the go-to angle
body: Most portraits in painting history and most character illustrations use some version of the three-quarter view. It shows the shape of the nose, the cheekbone and the jaw, which a front view flattens, while still letting the subject look at the viewer. The far side of the face shrinks and partly hides behind the nose and cheek, and that overlap is what makes the head feel round.
For bodies, a 3/4 turn also slims the silhouette and shows the depth of the chest and the outfit's side seams.

sections.h: How to draw a 3/4 view face

ol: Draw the head as a ball and curve the centre line around it, shifted toward the far side.
Wrap the eye line around the ball as a curve, not a straight line.
Place the near eye at full width and the far eye narrower, tucked against the nose bridge.
Cut a plane on the far side for the cheek and temple; the far cheek overlaps the far eye's outer corner slightly.
Put the near ear behind the jaw and leave the far ear hidden.

body: The classic mistake is drawing both eyes the same size, or placing the nose on a centre line that is still straight down the middle as if seen from the front.

sections.h: How to pose and photograph a 3/4 view
body: Ask the subject to turn the body about 45 degrees from the camera, then bring the face back partway. Light from the side the face is turned toward (short lighting) narrows the face and adds shape; light from the camera side (broad lighting) opens it up.

ul: Watch the far eye: if the nose crosses into it, the turn has gone too far for a 3/4 view.
Keep the eyes slightly toward the lens so more of the white shows on the far side.
Drop the near shoulder a little to lengthen the neck.

faq.a: A view of a head or body turned about 45 degrees from the viewer, between front view and profile, showing the near side fully and the far side partly.

faq.q: Why do the eyes look wrong in my 3/4 face?
faq.a: The far eye should be narrower and sit closer to the nose bridge, and the eye line should curve around the head.

faq.q: Is three-quarter view the same as half profile?
faq.a: They are used for the same idea, though half profile is sometimes used for a deeper turn closer to the side view.
